examples: They live in a huge house outside Dallas.
The difference in price was huge.
Thanks — that's a huge help.
The band is still huge in Japan.
Podcasts got huge in just a few years.
Winning that contract is huge for a small company like ours.

senses.head: Extremely large in size, amount or degree
examples: They live in a huge house outside Dallas.
The difference in price was huge.
Thanks — that's a huge help.

senses.head: Very popular, successful or important, informal
examples: The band is still huge in Japan.
Podcasts got huge in just a few years.
Winning that contract is huge for a small company like ours.

entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme, it already means very big: absolutely huge, really huge; huger and hugest exist but are rare — say much bigger or the biggest
entries.contrast: Huge already contains very, so very huge sounds like a learner: say really huge, absolutely huge or simply very big. A huge fan is someone who likes something a lot, not a large person.

examples: They rented a tiny apartment in Manhattan.
The print on the label was tiny.
She noticed even the tiniest mistake.
entries.comparison: -er/-est — tinier, tiniest
entries.contrast: Tiny is the extreme of small, so it goes more naturally with really or absolutely than with very, though very tiny is heard in speech. Americans often double it for effect: a tiny little dog, teeny-tiny. The y changes to i before -er and -est: tinier, tiniest.

entries.meaning: Extremely large in size, amount or degree. ---
examples: An enormous truck blocked the whole street.
The pressure on the team was enormous.
She's made an enormous difference at this school.
entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme: absolutely enormous, not very enormous; more enormous is rare — say even bigger
entries.contrast: Extreme, so not very enormous: say absolutely enormous or really enormous, and use the adverb enormously to intensify other words (enormously popular). The noun enormity is a trap: careful writers keep it for great wickedness (the enormity of the crime) and object to the enormity of the task when only size is meant.

entries.meaning: Extremely large; much bigger than usual. ---
examples: A gigantic wave crashed over the pier.
The new mall is gigantic.
We ordered a gigantic pizza for the whole team.
entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme: absolutely gigantic, not very gigantic
entries.contrast: Extreme, so not very gigantic. Giant also works as an adjective, but only before a noun (a giant step, giant waves); after be use gigantic or huge: The waves were gigantic, not The waves were giant.

examples: It's freezing out there — wear a hat.
We jumped into the freezing water of Lake Superior.
My hands are freezing.
Can you close the window? I'm freezing.
The kids came in from the snow freezing and hungry.
Freezing temperatures are expected in Atlanta tonight.
Drive carefully — there's freezing rain on the roads.

senses.head: Extremely cold, of the weather, a place, water or a part of the body
examples: It's freezing out there — wear a hat.
We jumped into the freezing water of Lake Superior.
My hands are freezing.

senses.head: Feeling very cold, of a person
examples: Can you close the window? I'm freezing.
The kids came in from the snow freezing and hungry.

senses.head: At or below 32°F (0°C), the temperature at which water turns to ice
examples: Freezing temperatures are expected in Atlanta tonight.
Drive carefully — there's freezing rain on the roads.

entries.position: both — sense 3 only before a noun (freezing rain, freezing temperatures)
entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme: absolutely freezing, not very freezing
entries.contrast: Extreme, so It's absolutely freezing, not very freezing. I'm freezing means I feel very cold; frozen food or a frozen lake has actually turned to ice. In freezing cold the word works like an adverb meaning extremely (freezing cold water). In the United States the freezing point in a forecast is 32°F.

examples: It's boiling in here — can we turn on the AC?
I was boiling in that wool sweater.
We waited two hours on a boiling sidewalk in Phoenix.
Drop the pasta into boiling water.
Pour the boiling water over the tea bags and wait three minutes.

senses.head: Extremely hot, of the weather, a place or a person, informal
examples: It's boiling in here — can we turn on the AC?
I was boiling in that wool sweater.
We waited two hours on a boiling sidewalk in Phoenix.

senses.head: Heated to the point where it bubbles and turns to steam
examples: Drop the pasta into boiling water.
Pour the boiling water over the tea bags and wait three minutes.

entries.position: both — the heat sense usually after be (It's boiling in here); the sense of water or oil at boiling point only before a noun (boiling water)
entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme: absolutely boiling, not very boiling
entries.contrast: Extreme, so not very boiling. Boiling water is still bubbling (Russian кипяток); boiled water has been boiled and may have cooled (кипячёная вода), and a boiled egg is cooked. In boiling hot and boiling mad the word works like an adverb meaning extremely.

examples: What's for dinner? I'm starving.
The kids were starving after soccer practice.
The charity sends food to starving families in the region.
Rescuers found the dogs cold and starving.
Small towns are starving for good jobs.
He was starving for someone to talk to.

senses.head: Very hungry, informal
examples: What's for dinner? I'm starving.
The kids were starving after soccer practice.

senses.head: Suffering or dying because there is not enough food
examples: The charity sends food to starving families in the region.
Rescuers found the dogs cold and starving.

senses.head: Wanting something very much because you have not had enough of it
examples: Small towns are starving for good jobs.
He was starving for someone to talk to.

entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme: absolutely starving, not very starving
entries.takes: for + noun — wanting something badly (starving for attention)
entries.contrast: I'm starving is everyday American for I'm very hungry, and nobody takes it literally. It is extreme, so not very starving: say I'm starving or I'm so hungry. For sense 3 the past participle is at least as common: starved for attention.

examples: My dad was furious when he saw the dent in the car.
She's furious with her brother for telling everyone.
Voters grew more furious about the tax increase every week.
The workers kept up a furious pace all week.
The storm hit the coast with furious force.
A furious debate broke out online.

senses.head: Extremely angry
examples: My dad was furious when he saw the dent in the car.
She's furious with her brother for telling everyone.
Voters grew more furious about the tax increase every week.

senses.head: Very fast, energetic or violent
examples: The workers kept up a furious pace all week.
The storm hit the coast with furious force.
A furious debate broke out online.

entries.comparison: more/most — more furious, most furious; extreme, so absolutely furious rather than very furious
entries.takes: at or with a person; about, over or at a thing; that-clause
entries.contrast: Furious already means very angry, so say absolutely furious or really furious, not very furious. The prepositions follow angry: furious at or with someone, furious about or over something. Sense 2 has nothing to do with anger — a furious pace is simply a very fast one.

examples: Thanks for dinner — the lasagna was delicious.
A delicious smell was coming from the kitchen.
That's the most delicious pie I've ever had.
There was a delicious irony in losing to his old team.
She had a delicious secret she couldn't wait to share.

senses.head: Having a very pleasant taste or smell
examples: Thanks for dinner — the lasagna was delicious.
A delicious smell was coming from the kitchen.
That's the most delicious pie I've ever had.

senses.head: Very pleasant or enjoyable
examples: There was a delicious irony in losing to his old team.
She had a delicious secret she couldn't wait to share.

entries.comparison: more/most — more delicious, most delicious; extreme, so absolutely delicious rather than very delicious
entries.contrast: Delicious is much stronger than tasty or good. Because it already means very tasty, really delicious and absolutely delicious sound natural and very delicious sounds like a learner.

examples: Her impression of our boss was hilarious.
We watched a hilarious video of a cat stealing a taco.
It was the most hilarious thing I'd seen all year.
entries.comparison: more/most — more hilarious, most hilarious; extreme, so absolutely hilarious, not very hilarious
entries.contrast: Hilarious means extremely funny, so very hilarious is wrong — say really hilarious or absolutely hilarious, or just very funny. It describes what makes people laugh, not how a person feels: The movie was hilarious, not I felt hilarious.

examples: The traffic on I-95 was awful this morning.
He was awful to his little sister.
It was the most awful week of my life.
I feel awful — I think I'm getting the flu.
You look awful. Go home and rest.
I feel awful about forgetting your birthday.
She felt awful that she couldn't help.
That's an awful lot of money for a used car.
He's gone to an awful lot of trouble for us.

senses.head: Very bad or unpleasant
examples: The traffic on I-95 was awful this morning.
He was awful to his little sister.
It was the most awful week of my life.

senses.head: Ill; not well
examples: I feel awful — I think I'm getting the flu.
You look awful. Go home and rest.

senses.head: Guilty or sorry about something
examples: I feel awful about forgetting your birthday.
She felt awful that she couldn't help.

senses.head: Very great in amount or degree, used for emphasis before a noun
examples: That's an awful lot of money for a used car.
He's gone to an awful lot of trouble for us.

entries.position: both — the 'very great' sense only before a noun (an awful lot)
entries.comparison: more/most — more awful, most awful; really awful or absolutely awful rather than very awful
entries.takes: about + noun or -ing — guilty or sorry (feel awful about it); to a person — unkind (awful to her); that-clause after it (It's awful that he lost his job)
entries.contrast: Awful and awesome both come from awe but now mean opposite things: awful is very bad, awesome is great. Americans also use awful as an adverb in speech (awful tired, awful nice); that is informal — in writing use awfully or really. An awful lot just means a very large amount and is not negative. Spelling: awful, never aweful.

examples: There was a terrible accident on the highway last night.
The food at that place is terrible.
It was the most terrible storm the town had ever seen.
I'm terrible at remembering names.
He's a terrible driver.
I feel terrible — I didn't sleep at all.
She looked terrible after the long flight.
I feel terrible about what I said to you.
He felt terrible that he'd missed her game.

senses.head: Very bad, unpleasant or serious; causing great harm, pain or fear
examples: There was a terrible accident on the highway last night.
The food at that place is terrible.
It was the most terrible storm the town had ever seen.

senses.head: Very bad at doing something; lacking skill
examples: I'm terrible at remembering names.
He's a terrible driver.

senses.head: Ill; not well
examples: I feel terrible — I didn't sleep at all.
She looked terrible after the long flight.

senses.head: Guilty or sorry about something
examples: I feel terrible about what I said to you.
He felt terrible that he'd missed her game.

entries.comparison: more/most — more terrible, most terrible; really terrible rather than very terrible
entries.takes: at + noun or -ing — bad at doing something (terrible at math); about — guilty or sorry (feel terrible about it); to a person — unkind
entries.contrast: The adverb terribly usually just means very and is not negative (terribly sorry, terribly important). Don't confuse terrible with terrific, which in American English means great (You did a terrific job), even though it looks related to terror. For skill use at: I'm terrible at math, not in math.

examples: You look fantastic!
We had a fantastic time in New Orleans.
Your presentation was fantastic.
Some players earn fantastic sums of money.
The company grew at a fantastic rate.
The book is full of fantastic creatures and talking animals.
He told some fantastic story about being chased by a bear.

senses.head: Extremely good; wonderful
examples: You look fantastic!
We had a fantastic time in New Orleans.
Your presentation was fantastic.

senses.head: Extremely large, of an amount
examples: Some players earn fantastic sums of money.
The company grew at a fantastic rate.

senses.head: Strange and imaginative, or too strange to be believed
examples: The book is full of fantastic creatures and talking animals.
He told some fantastic story about being chased by a bear.

entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme in the 'excellent' sense: absolutely fantastic, not very fantastic
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian фантастика is science fiction or fantasy — a sci-fi book is a science fiction novel, while a fantastic novel is just a wonderful one. In everyday American English fantastic almost always means excellent; sense 3 belongs to books, art and ideas. Extreme, so absolutely fantastic, not very fantastic.

entries.meaning: Extremely good; of very high quality. ---
examples: She speaks excellent Spanish.
The service at the hotel was excellent.
This park is excellent for little kids.
entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme: absolutely excellent or truly excellent, not very excellent; most excellent is a joke or a formal title
entries.takes: at + noun or -ing — very good at (excellent at chess); for — very well suited to (excellent for beginners)
entries.contrast: Excellent is already the top of good, so very excellent and more excellent are learner errors; to rank two excellent things, say one is even better. Excellent! on its own is a reply meaning great. Spelling: double l and -ent, not -ant.

examples: The bride looked gorgeous.
They have a gorgeous view of the bay.
She's the most gorgeous baby I've ever seen.
It's a gorgeous day — let's eat outside.
The weather in San Diego was gorgeous all week.

senses.head: Very beautiful or attractive
examples: The bride looked gorgeous.
They have a gorgeous view of the bay.
She's the most gorgeous baby I've ever seen.

senses.head: Very pleasant, of the weather, food or an experience
examples: It's a gorgeous day — let's eat outside.
The weather in San Diego was gorgeous all week.

entries.comparison: more/most — more gorgeous, most gorgeous; extreme, so absolutely gorgeous rather than very gorgeous
entries.contrast: Gorgeous is much stronger than pretty and is used for men as well as women (a gorgeous guy). Americans use it just as freely for weather, places and food, where it means wonderful. Extreme, so absolutely gorgeous or so gorgeous, not very gorgeous.

examples: Take off those filthy boots before you come in.
The bathroom at the gas station was filthy.
It was the filthiest kitchen the inspector had ever seen.
His mom told him to stop using such filthy language.
The comedian's jokes got filthier as the night went on.
Smoking is a filthy habit.
Get out of my house, you filthy liar!

senses.head: Extremely dirty
examples: Take off those filthy boots before you come in.
The bathroom at the gas station was filthy.
It was the filthiest kitchen the inspector had ever seen.

senses.head: Obscene or offensive, of words, jokes or pictures
examples: His mom told him to stop using such filthy language.
The comedian's jokes got filthier as the night went on.

senses.head: Very unpleasant or morally disgusting
examples: Smoking is a filthy habit.
Get out of my house, you filthy liar!

entries.comparison: -er/-est — filthier, filthiest
entries.contrast: Filthy is the extreme of dirty, so absolutely filthy, not very filthy. In filthy rich it works as an adverb meaning extremely and says nothing about dirt. For jokes and language the neutral word is dirty (a dirty joke); filthy is much stronger.

examples: Her kitchen is always spotless.
He wore a spotless white shirt to the interview.
The hotel room was spotless.
She has a spotless driving record.
The senator's reputation was spotless until the scandal.

senses.head: Perfectly clean
examples: Her kitchen is always spotless.
He wore a spotless white shirt to the interview.
The hotel room was spotless.

senses.head: Without any fault or bad mark
examples: She has a spotless driving record.
The senator's reputation was spotless until the scandal.

entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute: completely spotless, absolutely spotless, not very spotless
entries.contrast: Absolute, so very spotless is wrong — say spotless or spotlessly clean. Sense 2 goes mostly with record and reputation: a spotless driving record means no tickets and no accidents.

examples: We studied ancient Greece and Rome in sixth grade.
The museum has a room full of ancient Egyptian jewelry.
The town is built around an ancient oak tree.
These are some of the most ancient rocks on Earth.
The custom is ancient.
My laptop is ancient — it takes five minutes to start.
Don't ask him about TikTok; he's ancient.

senses.head: Belonging to the very distant past, especially to the civilizations before the fall of Rome
examples: We studied ancient Greece and Rome in sixth grade.
The museum has a room full of ancient Egyptian jewelry.

senses.head: Having existed for a very long time
examples: The town is built around an ancient oak tree.
These are some of the most ancient rocks on Earth.
The custom is ancient.

senses.head: Very old or old-fashioned, humorous
examples: My laptop is ancient — it takes five minutes to start.
Don't ask him about TikTok; he's ancient.

entries.position: both — sense 1 only before a noun (ancient Rome)
entries.comparison: more/most — more ancient, most ancient
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian античный is English ancient or classical (ancient Greece, classical art), while English antique means old and valuable, like furniture (антикварный). Ancient is not the everyday word for an old person — old or elderly is; calling someone ancient is a joke or an insult.

examples: The subway was packed at 8 a.m.
The band played to a packed stadium.
The restaurant is always packed on Fridays.
The guidebook is packed with useful tips.
The movie is packed with action from start to finish.
Are you packed yet? The cab's coming at six.
I'm all packed and ready to go.
Cars kept sliding on the packed snow.
The trail was packed dirt, hard as concrete.

senses.head: Extremely crowded
examples: The subway was packed at 8 a.m.
The band played to a packed stadium.
The restaurant is always packed on Fridays.

senses.head: Containing a lot of something
examples: The guidebook is packed with useful tips.
The movie is packed with action from start to finish.

senses.head: Having finished putting your things into bags for a trip
examples: Are you packed yet? The cab's coming at six.
I'm all packed and ready to go.

senses.head: Pressed down hard, of snow, soil or earth
examples: Cars kept sliding on the packed snow.
The trail was packed dirt, hard as concrete.

entries.position: both — sense 3 only after a verb (I'm all packed)
entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme: completely packed, absolutely packed or jam-packed, not very packed
entries.takes: with + noun — full of (packed with tourists, packed with vitamins)
entries.contrast: Packed already means very crowded, so very packed sounds wrong; Americans say packed, jam-packed or completely packed. Are you packed? asks whether someone has finished packing a suitcase, not whether they are in a crowd. Don't confuse it with packaged (packaged food, sold in a package).

examples: We got caught in the storm and came home soaked.
Take off those soaked socks.
His shirt was soaked through with sweat.
The film is soaked in nostalgia for the 1980s.
Boston is a city soaked in history.

senses.head: Completely wet
examples: We got caught in the storm and came home soaked.
Take off those soaked socks.
His shirt was soaked through with sweat.

senses.head: Full of a quality or feeling, literary
examples: The film is soaked in nostalgia for the 1980s.
Boston is a city soaked in history.

entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme: completely soaked, soaked through, not very soaked
entries.takes: through or to the skin — completely wet; in or with a liquid or a quality (soaked in sweat, soaked in history)
entries.contrast: Soaked is the extreme of wet, so not very soaked: say soaked, soaked through or soaking wet. In soaking wet the -ing form works like an adverb meaning completely. Before a noun it often forms a hyphenated compound: a blood-soaked shirt, a rain-soaked field.

examples: She was devastated by her father's death.
The players were devastated to lose in the final seconds.
Fans were devastated that the show was canceled.
Volunteers brought water to the devastated town.
After the hurricane, the whole coast looked devastated.

senses.head: Extremely shocked and upset
examples: She was devastated by her father's death.
The players were devastated to lose in the final seconds.
Fans were devastated that the show was canceled.

senses.head: Badly damaged or destroyed, of a place
examples: Volunteers brought water to the devastated town.
After the hurricane, the whole coast looked devastated.

entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme: absolutely devastated, completely devastated, not very devastated
entries.takes: by or at + noun — the cause (devastated by the news); to-infinitive (devastated to learn); that-clause
entries.contrast: -ed/-ing pair: the person is devastated; the news, loss or storm is devastating. Devastated means shocked and deeply hurt, far stronger than disappointed or sad — used about losing a game it is an exaggeration. Extreme, so not very devastated.

examples: My parents were ecstatic when I got into college.
She was ecstatic about the promotion.
Fans were ecstatic to see the band back together.
The saint wrote about his ecstatic visions.
The dancers moved in an ecstatic trance.

senses.head: Extremely happy and excited
examples: My parents were ecstatic when I got into college.
She was ecstatic about the promotion.
Fans were ecstatic to see the band back together.

senses.head: Relating to a state of intense religious or spiritual feeling, like a trance
examples: The saint wrote about his ecstatic visions.
The dancers moved in an ecstatic trance.

entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme: absolutely ecstatic, not very ecstatic
entries.takes: about, over or at + noun; to-infinitive; that-clause
entries.contrast: Russian экстатический suggests a trance or religious rapture; everyday American ecstatic just means thrilled: I'm ecstatic about the new job. Extreme, so absolutely ecstatic rather than very ecstatic.

examples: I'm petrified of snakes.
She was petrified to walk home alone after dark.
He stood there, petrified, as the bear came closer.
Arizona's Petrified Forest is full of ancient logs turned to stone.
The kids found a piece of petrified wood near the river.

senses.head: Extremely frightened, often too frightened to move
examples: I'm petrified of snakes.
She was petrified to walk home alone after dark.
He stood there, petrified, as the bear came closer.

senses.head: Turned slowly into stone over a very long time
examples: Arizona's Petrified Forest is full of ancient logs turned to stone.
The kids found a piece of petrified wood near the river.

entries.position: both — the fear sense mostly after be; before a noun it usually means turned to stone (petrified wood)
entries.comparison: not gradable — extreme: absolutely petrified, not very petrified
entries.takes: of + noun or -ing; to-infinitive; that-clause
entries.contrast: Petrified is the extreme of scared — so frightened you cannot move — so very petrified is wrong. The person is petrified; the experience is petrifying or terrifying.

examples: Her grandfather has been dead for ten years.
We found a dead bird on the porch.
Water the plants or they'll be dead by Friday.
My phone's dead — can I borrow your charger?
The car wouldn't start because the battery was dead.
The line suddenly went dead.
Downtown is dead after six o'clock.
Business has been dead all week.
He answered in a flat, dead voice.
Latin is a dead language.
After the vote, the bill is dead.
I slept on my arm, and now it's completely dead.
My legs went dead from sitting on the floor.
There was dead silence in the courtroom.
The arrow hit the dead center of the target.
The train came to a dead stop.
If Mom sees this mess, we're dead.
You're dead when Coach finds out.
After the double shift I was dead.
We were dead on our feet by the time the movers left.

senses.head: No longer alive
examples: Her grandfather has been dead for ten years.
We found a dead bird on the porch.
Water the plants or they'll be dead by Friday.

senses.head: Not working, especially because there is no power
examples: My phone's dead — can I borrow your charger?
The car wouldn't start because the battery was dead.
The line suddenly went dead.

senses.head: Very quiet, with no activity, energy or feeling
examples: Downtown is dead after six o'clock.
Business has been dead all week.
He answered in a flat, dead voice.

senses.head: No longer used, active or likely to happen
examples: Latin is a dead language.
After the vote, the bill is dead.

senses.head: Unable to feel anything, of a part of the body
examples: I slept on my arm, and now it's completely dead.
My legs went dead from sitting on the floor.

senses.head: Complete or exact, used before a noun
examples: There was dead silence in the courtroom.
The arrow hit the dead center of the target.
The train came to a dead stop.

senses.head: In serious trouble, informal
examples: If Mom sees this mess, we're dead.
You're dead when Coach finds out.

senses.head: Extremely tired, informal
examples: After the double shift I was dead.
We were dead on our feet by the time the movers left.

entries.position: both — the 'complete, exact' sense only before a noun (dead silence)
entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute: completely dead, almost dead; deader appears only in jokes
entries.contrast: Dead is the adjective, died the past of the verb, death the noun: He is dead or He died last year, never He is died. Something that kills is deadly, not dead (a deadly disease). As an adverb dead means completely or exactly — dead tired, dead serious, dead ahead — and has nothing to do with death. For a leg or foot that has lost feeling Americans more often say it fell asleep.

examples: Every snowflake is unique.
Each user gets a unique password.
This is a unique opportunity to work with NASA scientists.
The restaurant has a really unique atmosphere.
Her sense of style is pretty unique.
These birds are unique to the Galápagos Islands.
The problem isn't unique to our school.

senses.head: Being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else
examples: Every snowflake is unique.
Each user gets a unique password.
This is a unique opportunity to work with NASA scientists.

senses.head: Unusual or special, informal
examples: The restaurant has a really unique atmosphere.
Her sense of style is pretty unique.

senses.head: Belonging only to one particular person, place, group or thing
examples: These birds are unique to the Galápagos Islands.
The problem isn't unique to our school.

entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute in careful use: completely unique, almost unique; very unique and more unique are common in speech in sense 2, but editors and exams mark them wrong
entries.takes: to + noun — found only in or with (unique to Hawaii)
entries.contrast: Unique begins with a y sound, so it takes a: a unique chance, not an unique chance. In careful writing it means the only one of its kind, which cannot be more or less true, so very unique and rather unique are marked as errors; when you mean special, say unusual, rare or distinctive.

examples: She got a perfect score on the SAT.
Nobody's perfect.
It was a perfect fall day.
This dress is perfect for the wedding.
You'd be perfect for the job.
Six o'clock? That's perfect — thanks!
I told my life story to a perfect stranger on the plane.
What he said makes perfect sense.
English has three perfect tenses: past, present and future.
In perfect verb forms the helping verb is always a form of have.

senses.head: Having no mistakes or faults; as good as it can be
examples: She got a perfect score on the SAT.
Nobody's perfect.
It was a perfect fall day.

senses.head: Exactly right for a particular person, purpose or situation
examples: This dress is perfect for the wedding.
You'd be perfect for the job.
Six o'clock? That's perfect — thanks!

senses.head: Complete, used for emphasis before a noun
examples: I told my life story to a perfect stranger on the plane.
What he said makes perfect sense.

senses.head: In grammar, describing a verb tense made with a form of have and a past participle, which shows a completed action
examples: English has three perfect tenses: past, present and future.
In perfect verb forms the helping verb is always a form of have.

entries.position: both — senses 3 and 4 only before a noun (a perfect stranger, the perfect tenses)
entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute in careful use: absolutely perfect, almost perfect; more perfect has a long history (a more perfect Union, in the U.S. Constitution)
entries.takes: for + noun or -ing — exactly right for (perfect for a picnic)
entries.contrast: The adjective is stressed on the first syllable (PUR-fikt); the verb to perfect is stressed on the second (pur-FEKT). Perfect already means as good as possible, so very perfect is wrong; almost perfect and absolutely perfect are fine. In a perfect stranger and perfect sense it only adds emphasis — a perfect stranger is someone you have never met, not an ideal one.

examples: It's impossible to find parking downtown on Saturdays.
Finishing the whole report by Friday is impossible.
The snow made travel almost impossible.
The kids have been impossible all day.
Her boss put her in an impossible position.

senses.head: Not able to happen, exist or be done
examples: It's impossible to find parking downtown on Saturdays.
Finishing the whole report by Friday is impossible.
The snow made travel almost impossible.

senses.head: Very difficult to deal with or bear, of a person or situation
examples: The kids have been impossible all day.
Her boss put her in an impossible position.

entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute: completely impossible, almost impossible, nearly impossible, not very impossible
entries.takes: to-infinitive (impossible to find); for someone + to-infinitive (impossible for me to leave); that-clause after it (It's impossible that she knew)
entries.contrast: The situation, not the person, is impossible: It's impossible for me to come, not I am impossible to come. A person can be the subject only when the infinitive is about dealing with them (He's impossible to talk to), or on its own in sense 2 (My brother is impossible). Almost and nearly impossible are the natural way to soften it; very impossible is wrong.

examples: Water is essential for life.
Essential workers like nurses and grocery clerks kept working through the pandemic.
It's essential that you bring your passport.
The essential difference between the two plans is cost.
Honesty is an essential part of her character.
She adds a few drops of lavender essential oil to her bath.
Essential oils should never be swallowed.

senses.head: Completely necessary
examples: Water is essential for life.
Essential workers like nurses and grocery clerks kept working through the pandemic.
It's essential that you bring your passport.

senses.head: Basic and most important; forming the central part of something
examples: The essential difference between the two plans is cost.
Honesty is an essential part of her character.

senses.head: Taken from a plant and carrying its smell or flavor, of an oil
examples: She adds a few drops of lavender essential oil to her bath.
Essential oils should never be swallowed.

entries.position: both — sense 2 mostly before a noun; sense 3 only in essential oil
entries.comparison: not gradable — absolutely essential, not very essential; most essential is common in speech in the sense 'most basic'
entries.takes: to or for + noun (essential to success, essential for growth); to-infinitive after it (It's essential to book early); that-clause, often with the base form of the verb (It's essential that he be there)
entries.contrast: Essential is much stronger than important: it means you cannot do without it. After It is essential that, formal American English uses the base verb: It's essential that every student attend, not attends. Essential oil is Russian эфирное масло, and the essentials (a noun) are the basic things you need.

examples: My sister is pregnant with twins.
Pregnant women should check with a doctor before taking any medicine.
She got pregnant right after the wedding.
There was a pregnant pause before she answered.
His silence was pregnant with meaning.

senses.head: Carrying a developing baby inside the body
examples: My sister is pregnant with twins.
Pregnant women should check with a doctor before taking any medicine.
She got pregnant right after the wedding.

senses.head: Full of meaning or unspoken feeling
examples: There was a pregnant pause before she answered.
His silence was pregnant with meaning.

entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute: six months pregnant; very pregnant is a joke meaning late in pregnancy and clearly showing
entries.takes: with a baby (pregnant with twins); by the father; with meaning or feeling, literary (sense 2)
entries.contrast: Say She is pregnant or She is expecting, not She is in pregnancy; for becoming pregnant Americans say get pregnant. The length of time goes before the adjective: She's seven months pregnant. Absolute, so very pregnant is only a joke.

examples: Are you married?

She kept her married name after the divorce.

senses.head: Having a husband or wife
examples: Are you married?
They've been married for thirty years.
A young married couple lives next door.

senses.head: Relating to marriage or to a husband and wife
examples: They were still getting used to married life.
She kept her married name after the divorce.

senses.head: Completely devoted to something and unwilling to give it up
examples: He's married to his job.
The mayor isn't married to the plan; she's open to changes.

entries.position: both — sense 2 only before a noun (married life)
entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute: happily married, newly married, not more married
entries.takes: to a person — never with or on (married to a doctor); to a job or an idea — devoted to it
entries.contrast: Use to: She's married to a teacher, not with or on (Russian замужем за, женат на). Married with children is a different pattern — married and having children. Be married is the state and get married the event: We got married in 2019 and We've been married for five years, not We are married for five years. English has one word for both женат and замужем.

Am I correct in thinking you two have met?

senses.head: Right or true; without mistakes
examples: Is this the correct address?
Your answer is correct.
Choose the most correct answer from the list.

senses.head: Right in what you think or say, of a person
examples: You're absolutely correct.
Am I correct in thinking you two have met?

senses.head: Following the accepted rules of behavior or of a situation
examples: What's the correct way to address a senator?
His manners were always correct but cold.

entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute in the 'right' sense, but more correct and most correct are common when comparing how accurate something is (the most correct answer)
entries.takes: in + -ing — right to think so (correct in assuming); to-infinitive (You were correct to call)
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian корректный usually means polite or tactful — in English say polite, courteous or respectful. English correct behavior means following the accepted rules, as in politically correct. You're correct is more formal than You're right. The verb correct (to fix mistakes) looks and sounds the same.

senses.head: Having all the parts it should have; whole
examples: We finally have a complete set of the Harry Potter books.
The list isn't complete — we're missing three names.
This is the most complete collection of her letters.

senses.head: Finished
examples: Work on the new bridge is almost complete.
Your registration is not complete until you pay the fee.

senses.head: Total, used for emphasis before a noun
examples: The meeting was a complete waste of time.
I felt like a complete idiot.
She's a complete stranger to me.

senses.head: Including something as an extra part, after a noun
examples: The apartment comes complete with a washer and dryer.
He showed up dressed as Santa, complete with a white beard.

entries.position: both — sense 3 only before a noun (a complete stranger); complete with follows its noun
entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute when it means finished, but more complete and most complete are normal for having more of the parts (a more complete list)
entries.takes: with + noun — including something extra (a kitchen complete with dishwasher)
entries.contrast: Complete is both an adjective and a verb: The work is complete (done) and They completed the work. A completed form is one someone has filled out. In a complete idiot or complete nonsense it only adds emphasis, like total. Complete with is a description pattern that comes after the noun: a house complete with a pool.

examples: The total cost of the trip was about $3,000.
What's the total number of students in the program?
The party was a total disaster.
There was total silence in the room.
I felt like a total fool.

senses.head: Including everything; being the whole amount
examples: The total cost of the trip was about $3,000.
What's the total number of students in the program?

senses.head: Complete, used for emphasis
examples: The party was a total disaster.
There was total silence in the room.
I felt like a total fool.

entries.position: attributive only — in both senses; after be only in formal writing about sense 2 (The destruction was total)
entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute
entries.contrast: Total goes before its noun: The total cost is $50, not The cost is total $50. After a verb Americans use the noun or the verb: The total is $50, The bill totals $50. In informal American English the verb total also means to wreck a car completely: He totaled his car (one l). The adverb totally in speech often just means completely or yes: I totally agree.

senses.head: Containing nothing, or with no people in it
examples: The fridge is empty — we need to go shopping.

senses.head: Without meaning, value or real intention
examples: Voters are tired of empty promises.
His threats turned out to be empty.

senses.head: Feeling that life has no meaning or purpose, of a person
examples: She felt empty for months after the divorce.
Winning didn't make him happy; he just felt empty.

entries.comparison: -er/-est — emptier, emptiest
entries.takes: of + noun — formal, without (streets empty of cars)
entries.contrast: Russian пустой covers more than English empty. A page or form with nothing written on it is blank; a seat nobody is using is free (Is this seat taken?); an apartment or a job with nobody in it is vacant. Empty is also a verb (empty the dishwasher). Although it sounds absolute, almost empty, emptier and emptiest are all normal.

senses.head: Containing as much or as many as it can hold, or a lot of something
examples: The parking lot was full, so we parked on the street.

senses.head: Having eaten enough; not hungry
examples: I'm full — I can't eat another bite.

senses.head: Complete, whole or as great as possible
examples: Please write your full name.

We got a full refund.

senses.head: Busy, with a lot of activities
examples: I have a really full schedule this week.
She lived a long and full life.

senses.head: Round and large, of the face, lips or body; wide, of clothing
examples: She has full lips and dark eyes.
The dress has a full skirt.
The brand makes jeans for a fuller figure.

senses.head: Rich and strong, of a sound, taste or color
examples: The wine has a full, fruity flavor.

entries.position: both — with of it can follow the noun (a room full of people)
entries.comparison: -er/-est — fuller, fullest
entries.takes: of + noun — containing a lot (full of water, full of ideas); of oneself — too proud
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian полный about a person often means overweight, but English I'm full means I'm not hungry any more: No dessert, thanks — I'm full. For weight say heavy or overweight; a fuller figure is only a polite fashion phrase. Full of follows its noun naturally: a box full of toys. The suffix -ful has one l: careful, spoonful. To the fullest means as much as possible (live life to the fullest).

examples: The final chapter surprised everyone.

The judge's decision is final.

senses.head: Coming at the end; last in a series
examples: The final chapter surprised everyone.
She scored in the final minute of the game.
This is your final warning.

senses.head: Not able to be changed or argued about
examples: The judge's decision is final.
Is that your final answer?

entries.position: both — sense 1 only before a noun (the final chapter)
entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute
entries.contrast: Final and last overlap in sense 1, but final stresses that nothing comes after: the final episode. After be, final has sense 2: The decision is final means it cannot be changed, not that it came last. The adverb finally usually means after a long time (She finally called). The finals (a noun) are the last games of a tournament or end-of-term exams.

senses.head: Involving or done by everyone in a group or in the world
examples: The plan has universal support among the teachers.

senses.head: True or found everywhere and in every case
examples: Music is a universal language.

senses.head: Able to be used with all or most types of something, of a device
examples: I lost the universal remote again.

entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute: almost universal, nearly universal; more universal occurs, meaning more widespread
entries.contrast: Russian универсальный often means versatile — for a person or tool that can do many things say versatile or all-purpose (a versatile actor, an all-purpose cleaner), not universal. English universal means for everyone or everywhere; the 'fits everything' sense lives in a few set phrases: universal remote, universal adapter.

examples: Is the universe infinite?

senses.head: Without limits or an end
examples: Is the universe infinite?
There are an infinite number of points on a line.
The set of whole numbers is infinite.

senses.head: Very great, as if without limit
examples: The teacher showed infinite patience with the class.
She wrapped the old photos with infinite care.

entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute; to compare, use the adverb: infinitely better
entries.contrast: Pronunciation trap: finite is FY-nyt, but infinite is IN-fuh-nuht — the stress moves and both vowels change. Don't confuse it with the grammar term infinitive (to go). Infinite is absolute, so very infinite is wrong; to compare use infinitely (infinitely more complicated).

examples: Cut the cake into eight equal pieces.
One kilometer is equal to about 0.62 miles.
The two bedrooms are equal in size.
The Declaration of Independence says that all men are created equal.
Women are still fighting for equal pay.
They're equal partners in the business.

senses.head: The same in size, amount, number or value
examples: Cut the cake into eight equal pieces.
One kilometer is equal to about 0.62 miles.
The two bedrooms are equal in size.

senses.head: Having the same rights, status or opportunities
examples: The Declaration of Independence says that all men are created equal.
Women are still fighting for equal pay.
They're equal partners in the business.

senses.head: Having the ability or strength to deal with something
examples: She proved equal to the challenge.
I wasn't sure he was equal to the job.

entries.comparison: not gradable — absolute; more equal is a famous joke from Orwell's Animal Farm (some animals are more equal than others)
entries.takes: to + noun — the same as (equal to one mile); to a task — able to do it; in + noun — the way they are the same (equal in size)
entries.contrast: Use equal to, not equal with, for amounts: One yard is equal to three feet. In math Americans usually use the verb: Two plus two equals four. Equal is about size, value or rights; for things that are exactly alike use the same: We have the same car, not equal cars. As a noun, an equal is a person of the same rank (She treated us as equals).
